transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-12
Start time: 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Sarah Nguyen (AcmePay CTO), Tom Alvarez (AcmePay Lead SRE), Priya Desai (AcmePay ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC sync to review latency tuning results. Focus on TTFT, streaming vs batched behavior, sequence length distribution, and kernel choices (FlashAttention/triton/int8). Action items agreed: share benchmarks, run wider TTFT sampling, schedule kernel deep-dive.

Topics: TTFT numbers, streaming implementation artifacts, sequence length impact, kernel selection and quantization tradeoffs, production rollout considerations (dedicated vs hosted), next steps for benchmarking.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for hopping on. Quick roll call; Maya and I from Redwood, and Sarah, Tom, Priya from AcmePay, right?
[00:12] Sarah: Yep that's right. Hi Jordan, Maya. Thanks.
[00:15] Maya: Hey. Quick agenda — run through last week's benchmark, dig into the TTFT delta when streaming's on, look at sequence length tail, and then kernel/quantization next steps. Sound good?
[00:28] Tom: Sounds good. We saw a pretty big p99 spike on the last demo so want to understand root cause.
[00:33] Maya: Totally. I pulled the run from Friday — config uses FP16, int8 quant profile for the final stage, and streaming-enabled with 16ms chunk delay. We also tried a non-streaming batched run at 64 batch size.
[00:47] Priya: Quick note — our production prompt distribution is heavy on shorter sequences, median ~48 tokens, 95th ~420 tokens. So the tail matters but 90% are under 128.
[00:59] Jordan: Great that's useful. Maya, can you call out the TTFT numbers?
[01:04] Maya: Yep. For the streaming run the TTFT p50 was ~28ms, p90 ~82ms, p99 ~210ms. For the batched non-streaming run (64 batch) TTFT p50 was 62ms, p90 180ms, p99 480ms. So streaming improved p50 significantly but we still see these p99 outliers.
[01:22] Sarah: Those p99s line up with what we saw — occasionally a request took half a second to first token which breaks the UX.
[01:30] Tom: Right and on SRE side we saw some correlation with big sequence requests — the KV cache filling and then eviction causing spikes. Could be memory pressure on the backend nodes.
[01:40] Maya: Yeah that's one hypothesis. Another is kernel fallback: some long sequences triggered a slower attention kernel path — our runtime will pick between FlashAttention-optimized kernels and a fallback that handles larger context or certain dims. If the model goes past a tuned window we can hit a non-optimized codepath.
[01:58] Priya: Is that the triton fallback path you mentioned earlier? Sometimes the profiler shows a few kernels using slower triton loops.
[02:04] Maya: Exactly. The scheduling will pick fast fused kernels when shapes are friendly; otherwise it uses generic triton kernels which are slower. Also quantization mode can influence kernel choice — int8 paths sometimes force different memory layouts.
[02:19] Sarah: Do you have a way to force the kernel selection or pin to a particular kernel family for the POC? That would be helpful to isolate.
[02:27] Maya: We can. For the POC we can toggle kernel policies per model variant. I'll include the exact flags in the benchmark sheet I send. For example we can limit sequence length per shard or force FlashAttention for up to 512 seq if memory allows, or allow the fallback beyond that.
[02:45] Tom: Memory pressure — we are running on instance type with 48GB VRAM and typically run two shards per gpu. If a big request comes in it can cause KV cache blowout. Any suggestions?
[02:55] Maya: A few levers: reduce max concurrent beams per replica, aggressive prefix KV caching for repeated user prompts, or set soft limits on request length with graceful truncation. Also autoscale burst capacity on Dedicated so long requests are routed to less loaded machines.
[03:12] Jordan: On the Dedicated vs Hosted question — for the pilot you're on Hosted, right? AcmePay's POC is hosted with reserved concurrency?
[03:20] Sarah: We're on Redwood hosted test cluster with some reserved capacity. If Dedicated reduces these spikes it's fine but we want to understand tuning first.
[03:28] Maya: Understood. Back to TTFT: we also saw an impact from the chunking parameter we used for streaming — 16ms vs 32ms chunk delay. The higher chunk delay reduced CPU overhead but increased TTFT. So there's tradeoff.
[03:42] Priya: Did you measure token emission latency vs first token? Our concern is perceived latency — first token matters most.
[03:48] Maya: Yes, we recorded both. Time-to-first-token (TTFT) and per-token throughput. With streaming the initial token can be emitted as soon as the first attention pass completes, whereas in batched mode you wait for the whole batch. So streaming reduces TTFT but if kernels block due to large seq it still spikes.
[04:06] Tom: Are you seeing any GC or host-side spikes? I noticed host CPU sometimes hits 90% during the p99 events.
[04:12] Maya: We saw a correlation with CUDA memcpy stalls in a couple of runs; likely due to bursts of KV writes. Could be due to our logging/tracing hooks enabled in that run — I had high debug tracing on which I shouldn't have. Sorry, that was my fault.
[04:25] Jordan: Noted — maybe we should re-run with tracing off to get a clean baseline.
[04:29] Maya: Agreed.
[04:30] Sarah: Yes please. Also Priya mentioned median short sequences — can you show us the sequence length distribution graph?
[04:36] Maya: I'll drop it in the sheet but quick verbal: about 60% under 64 tokens, 30% between 64 and 256, and 10% tail up to 1k. The p99s line up with that 10%.
[04:49] Priya: For our application, the long ones are important for auditing contexts. We can't just truncate them aggressively.
[04:55] Maya: Understood. Two practical options: enable selective offload for very long sequences (send them to larger memory machines), or pre-process to chunk long contexts into multiple shorter queries with context stitching client-side. Both have tradeoffs.
[05:08] Tom: The selective offload is interesting — does Redwood support routing by sequence-length policy?
[05:14] Maya: Yes, we have smart routing. We can route by policy to a pool of high-memory nodes (dedicated) when seq_len > 512. That routing adds network hop but prevents local KV thrash.
[05:25] Jordan: Also note caching — if a big sequence shares prefixes across requests, KV caching saves a lot.
[05:31] Priya: We do have repeated prefixes in some flows. Worth testing.
[05:34] Sarah: Can you remind us what quantization profile you used? You said int8 for the final stage.
[05:40] Maya: We generated a symmetric int8 calibration for weights with per-channel scales on activations. That gave ~2x throughput improvement on some kernels but caused slightly different memory layout which triggered fallback kernels for some ops.
[05:53] Priya: So int8 helped throughput but may have caused kernel selection to shift and introduced p99s.
[05:58] Maya: Exactly. It's a tradeoff — better average throughput, potential worse tail depending on kernel coverage.
[06:05] Tom: What's your recommendation for the POC next step? Prioritize stable TTFT over raw throughput?
[06:12] Jordan: From a UX POV, I'd prioritize TTFT and p99 stability. You can allow some throughput loss initially, then iterate to regain it.
[06:20] Maya: Proposed plan: 1) re-run baseline with tracing off and pinned kernel policy (force fast kernels up to 512) 2) run streaming with 8ms chunk delay and 16ms as comparison 3) run int8 vs fp16 toggles but keep kernel policy pinned to observe pure quant impact. Also collect 1k TTFT samples for each config.
[06:44] Sarah: That sounds good. Can you also include the exact kernel flags? Our infra team will want to replicate.
[06:50] Maya: Yes I'll include the command line and config blob. I'll also add note about the fallback detection logs so you can grep for "fallback_kernel" events.
[06:59] Tom: Regarding autoscaling — if we hit a spike, can Dedicated burst capacity help immediately?
[07:05] Jordan: Dedicated burst is designed for that; you get additional nodes in a few minutes. For strict p99 SLOs you want some baseline headroom or synchronous fallback to a simpler model to preserve response.
[07:18] Priya: Would a simpler smaller model reduce p99s? We can run a fallback to a smaller quantized model for very long sequences.
[07:26] Maya: Yes that's a common pattern — model variant fallback (lower quality) for tail requests; Redwood can route automatically. But you need to validate quality impact.
[07:36] Sarah: Ok so action items: re-run clean benchmarks, share configs and kernel flags, run 1k TTFT with streaming. Anything else?
[07:44] Jordan: We'll also send a short doc on routing policy examples and recommended instance types for 512+ seq.
[07:51] Maya: I'll add logs to help detect kernel fallbacks and include the exact flags.
[07:55] Tom: We'll run the TTFT batch and share results.
[07:58] Priya: One more question — did you try batching + streaming hybrid? Like small initial streaming chunk then accumulate in a small batch for subsequent tokens?
[08:07] Maya: We experimented with micro-batching: emit first token immediately then batch the next few requests over a 5-10ms window. It reduces overhead and keeps TTFT low for first token, but complexity increases on server side. We can run that test too.
[08:22] Sarah: Sounds valuable, please include it in the benchmark matrix.
[08:26] Jordan: Great. Any blockers on our side?
[08:29] Tom: None other than scheduling the tests. We should be able to run them this week.
[08:33] Sarah: Alright, thanks.
[08:35] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll recap and follow-up with the sheet and kernel flags.
[08:40] Maya: I'll send the spreadsheet by Friday (2026-05-14) and include the exact CI commands, kernel flags, and which runs had tracing on.
[08:48] Sarah: Perfect. Talk soon.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard tokens (e.g., "KV cash" instead of "KV cache"), some speaker attributions may be slightly off.
